Dhantal源自印度，由印度契約勞工在加勒比海地區創製，常見於圭亞那、蘇利南、: The dhantal comes from India and was created by Indian indentured labourers in the Caribbean; it is common in Guyana, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago, other parts of the Caribbean and Fiji. It developed from the iron bow of the ox-cart used on the plantations into an idiophone of a long steel rod, whose upper end may be blunt or taper to a fine point to increase resonance and whose lower end is bent into a circle and set on the floor or a table. The early beater was a horseshoe, and the modern one keeps that shape. Its name means literally 'stick-strike rhythm', formed from 'stick' and 'to strike rhythmically', and it provides a clear beat in Indo-Caribbean music such as chutney, baithak gana and taan singing.

The dhantal (also dandtal) is an idiophone of a long steel rod, sounding much like a triangle. Its form derives from the ox-cart iron bow used on plantations in Guyana, Suriname, Trinidad and Tobago, other parts of the Caribbean and Fiji; the lower end is bent into a circle and the instrument rests on the floor or a table when played, while the upper end may be blunt or tapered to a point to increase resonance. The source names no clear family, marking it only as an idiophone. The player holds the rod in the weaker hand and the horseshoe-shaped beater in the strong hand, controlling resonance by opening and closing the palm that holds the rod, and gives a clear beat. It was developed in the Caribbean by Indian indentured labourers and is used in Indo-Caribbean music such as chutney, baithak gana and taan singing.

The lower end of the rod is bent into a circle and can rest on the floor, a table or another surface. It sounds as a metallic stroke, and opening and closing the holding hand controls how long the resonance lasts. A beginner should first fix the lower end and practise a steady grip and stroke, then play the fixed figure of two semiquavers followed by one quaver to mark the beat and help the ensemble keep time.
